Your Instructor: Dr. Juls Gilliam, D.Sc. — “Dr. G”

Welcome to the workshop.

This class is a workshop where we build machines out of nothing but text. No wood, no metal, no tools you can hold. Just HTML for the structure, CSS for the style, and your own hands on the keyboard.

By the end of the semester you will have designed, built, and published a five-page website of your own. Every part of it will be something you made yourself. Read this handbook all the way through — there is 1 extra credit point waiting at the bottom for students who do.

Read this before anything else

This Is Not a Teach-Yourself Online Class

You have probably taken an online course that handed you a textbook, a due date, and a shrug. That is not this course.

I post a lecture every week, and you write the code with me while it plays. Not watch it and try it later — open your editor, hit play, and build alongside me. Pause when you need to. Rewind when you miss something. Type every line yourself. By the time the video ends you should have working code in front of you, not notes about working code.

Every lecture is built on the one before it. Week 6 assumes week 5 is already in your hands. That makes falling behind more dangerous here than in a normal online class: a missed week is not one missed assignment, it is the floor the next four weeks stand on. Skip it and everything after it gets harder for reasons that have nothing to do with how smart you are.

So do not get behind — and if you do, reach out immediately. Not at the end of the module. Not when grades post. The moment you feel the gap opening. I can fix a one-week gap in a single conversation. A five-week gap takes the rest of the semester.

How I know you are okay

During the lecture, tell me you understand the material. A comment, a reply, a message — whatever the lecture asks for. That one line is how I take attendance in a class where I cannot see your face.

And if you do not understand it, tell me that instead. Say it right there in the lecture, or email me. Either answer is completely fine. Silence is the only answer I cannot work with — because from where I sit, a student who is lost and a student who is fine look exactly the same until it is too late to help.

Introductions

Meet Patch

That purple robot you keep running into is Patch. He is the mascot of this course, and he is not decoration.

Patch is this whole class in one character. He is built out of spare parts. He is always mid‑repair. And his entire philosophy is that a broken connection is not a dead end — it is just something to patch. That is web development. Your page will break. Mine breaks too. You find the loose wire, you fix it, you keep going.

He wears goggles because he looks closely at things. He carries a tablet full of HTML because he is still learning it, same as you. And he keeps his headphones around his neck rather than over his ears, because he came here to talk to people.

When Patch shows up in this handbook, he is marking something worth slowing down for: a rule that matters, help that already exists and is free, or a reminder that you are not building this alone. Say hi when you see him. He waves back.

If I Need to Reach You

Let’s Talk Instead of Typing

Email is fine for quick questions. For anything with feeling, history, or confusion attached to it, email is where miscommunication starts. Tone does not travel well in writing, and a thread that could have been a five-minute call turns into three days of back-and-forth.

So if something is complicated, ask me for a phone call or a Zoom meeting. I would much rather talk it through with you and settle it in one conversation. I will make the time.

Come to me first.

If something in this course is not working — a grade you do not understand, a policy that feels unfair, a deadline you cannot meet, or something I said that landed wrong — bring it to me before you take it anywhere else.

Give me the chance to fix it. I can almost always solve a problem I know about, and most of them are settled in a single conversation. I cannot fix something I never heard about.

6. The Blueprint — What You’ll Learn

Four skills you will walk out of this class with.

1. Read the plans
Describe and use current web page technologies: modern HTML5 and CSS standards, responsive design, and accessible web practices.
2. Do the building
Use a code editor to write HTML and CSS: build well-structured pages, organize your files, and apply styles using external or internal CSS.
3. Judge good design
Discuss, recognize, and apply the elements of good design: layout, typography, color, hierarchy, alignment, spacing, and usability.
4. Put it online
Describe and use common web servers: publish and test webpages using hosting tools, and understand how browsers get content from servers.

The Official Course Objectives

The four cards above are how I say it. Below is how the College says it — these are the approved outcomes for ITD 110, word for word. Upon completing the course, the student will be able to:

  • Describe and use current web page creation technologies
  • Use text editors to write HTML and CSS code
  • Discuss, recognize, and apply the elements of good design
  • Describe and use common web servers

Major Topics We Will Cover

Thirteen topics, spread across the fifteen modules in The Route Map. Every one of them shows up in your final website.

1Getting started with HTML and CSS
2Formatting text
3Creating hypertext links
4Using color and graphics
5Using tables
6Creating user-friendly navigation
7Working with HTML forms
8Working with Cascading Style Sheets
9Designing HTML and CSS for multiple devices (Responsive Design)
10Incorporating audio and video elements
11Publishing to a web server using FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
12Understanding the implications of copyrights on web design
13Knowledge of the basics of accessibility as it relates to web design

8. The Machine — How the Course Works

Five moving parts. They all work together.

  1. Readings — articles and visual guides that introduce the main ideas.
  2. Weekly lecture videos — you write the code along with me while the video plays. Not watching. Building.
  3. Practice — hands-on exercises that build your skills.
  4. Projects — larger web assignments where you apply what you learned.
  5. Final Project — your finished website, built and published by you.

About Your Assignments

You will create original web content, including graphics, audio, video, and interactive elements. Projects are graded on creativity, usability, and accessibility.

9. Full Steam — Communication (15%)

A quiet engine can still be running hot. What matters is that the wheels turn.

You can communicate out loud or in writing. Your score is not based on how often you speak. It is based on taking part in the course and showing real progress on your web design skills.

Communication goes both ways.

Answer me within 24 to 48 hours. I hold myself to 24–48 hours on your messages, Monday through Friday. The same clock applies to you. If I email, message, or call you about your work, your attendance, or a grade, reply inside that window — even if the whole reply is “Got it, I will send it Friday.” Silence is the one answer that costs you points.

Read your feedback, then tell me you read it. Every graded assignment comes back with comments. Open them, read them, and reply in Canvas or by email to confirm you received them. Feedback you never opened is feedback that never happened — and acknowledging it is part of this grade.

How You Earn Communication Points

  • Talking about your pages — what you built, what you changed, and why.
  • Explaining your design choices — layout, fonts, color, hierarchy, and accessibility.
  • Describing your technical work — HTML structure, CSS styling, file organization, links and navigation, images, and fixing problems.
  • Talking about what went wrong — and how you fixed it.
  • Asking and answering questions — during demos, lab time, or peer review, about your work or a classmate’s.
  • Working with feedback — giving useful feedback, and using the feedback you get.
  • Replying within 24 to 48 hours — when I reach out about your work, your attendance, or a grade.
  • Opening your graded feedback and confirming you read it — a one-line reply in Canvas or by email is enough.
  • Being findable — logging into Canvas regularly, posting when a discussion asks for it, and answering when I reach out.
  • Being present and working — following the demonstrations and examples, working steadily each week, and asking for help when you need it.

Different Ways to Communicate

  • Posting in discussions — sharing progress, explaining choices, asking questions
  • Small-group discussion or peer review in Canvas
  • Written responses or short reflections
  • Canvas discussions or submissions
  • One-on-one conversations at Zoom or in-person office hours
  • Proof of progress — drafts, revisions, screenshots, notes, checklists, or a short “what I changed” summary

Remember: the quality of your communication matters more than the amount.

How Communication Is Scored

The three levels of communication and what each one looks like in practice.
Level What It Looks Like
Full Steam
Exceeds Expectations (A)		 Takes part regularly in discussions and peer review, explains design decisions clearly, uses feedback, answers messages promptly, and communicates professionally.
Steady Pressure

Course Conduct

This course values your experience and curiosity. At the same time, I am responsible for the direction of the course and for instructional decisions. Please engage respectfully in discussions, comments, and messages. That behavior may affect your communication and conduct evaluation.

Walking Into the Room — Online

  • Say hello in the first week. Post in the introduction discussion and send me one message so I know who you are. In a face-to-face class I would meet you at the door; online, this is the door.
  • Log in and be seen. An online class where nobody hears from you looks exactly like an empty chair. Check Canvas several times a week, not once on Sunday night.
  • Write like a person, to a person. Start messages with a greeting, sign your name, and use your NOVA email. Tone travels badly in text, so give me — and your classmates — the benefit of the doubt, and I will do the same for you.
  • Do not go quiet. Disappearing is the one thing I cannot work with. If you are behind, overwhelmed, or lost, send me one honest sentence. That is all it takes to keep this fixable.

This is not about formality. Online, the only way I know you are here is that you show up in the work and in the inbox. A student I hear from is a student I can help; a student I never hear from is a name in a gradebook. Be the first one.

Contributing vs. Competing

Many of you arrive with real experience — a job in IT, a side business, a language you already write, a tutorial you have already finished. That experience makes this class better and I want it in the discussions. Bring it.

There is a difference, though, between adding to a lesson and competing with it. Adding sounds like “I have seen this done another way — can I show it?” Competing looks like correcting the instructor in a public thread to see who wins. The first one teaches everybody something. The second one derails the thread and spends everyone’s time.

What does not work is running commentary under every lesson, repeatedly redirecting a discussion, or treating the course as a contest. There are many valid ways to build a page. In here we build it the way I am teaching it first, because the assignment is graded on the method as much as on the result — then you are free to show me yours.

Web development changes every single year and nobody knows all of it, me included. In this course, being the person who helps everyone else understand something is worth far more than being the person who was right first.

If this does not work for you. If you have concerns about the communication expectations, or you need a different way to show that you are engaged, contact me early in the semester. There is more than one path here.

10. The Big Build — Your Final Project

A website you build from scratch, in Visual Studio Code, by yourself.

The Assignment

Build a working, original website from scratch using Visual Studio Code only. No other editors are allowed. You need five pages: Home, About, Gallery, Services, and Contact. If you want to rename a page, ask me first.

Design Standards

  • A hero image on the Home page.
  • Every page works well on phones as well as computers.
  • Every image must be made by you.
  • Use good visual design and keep your contrast strong.
  • Use the same fonts, colors, spacing, and layout across all pages.

Required Features

Video
Embed or upload a video. See the Canva video tutorial.
Table
For example, a timeline or a pricing table.
Lists
Include both a bulleted list and a numbered list.
Images
Banner and hero images across your pages.
Slideshow
An image slideshow on at least one page.
Form
A working contact form: name, email, and message.

Accessibility & Quality (Required)

  • Use semantic HTML tags: header, nav, main, section, and footer.
  • Write alt text for every image.
  • Use link text that describes where the link goes.
  • Use media queries so the site works on mobile.
  • Your site must pass W3C HTML and CSS validation.

What Goes on Each Page

The five required pages and what each one must contain.
Page What It Needs
HomeA welcome message, an introduction, a hero image, and a call-to-action button.
AboutA banner image, paragraphs about you or your mission, a bulleted list, and a table (a timeline or other useful information).
GalleryA grid of images, an embedded video, and captions that describe each item.
ServicesA numbered list of services, an icon or image for each one, and a pricing table that works on mobile.
ContactA working contact form (name, email, message), a Google Maps embed if you want one, and social media icons.

How to Turn It In

  • Submit a link to your hosted website, or use the method posted in Canvas.
  • Your site must open correctly, and every page must be reachable through your navigation.
  • Along with the link, write a short summary of the decisions you made and why — layout, color, type, and accessibility — in your own words.

Stuck? Message me in the Canvas Inbox early. Do not wait until the due date.

11. Boiler Room Rules — Course Policies

Not the fun part. Still the part that protects your grade.

Learning is a team effort between you and me. I will give you structured activities that help you master the material. You are expected to take part fully, meet deadlines, and reach out early when something is wrong.

Attendance in an Online Class

Showing up is still the single strongest predictor of passing this course. Online, “showing up” means logging in and doing the work every week — and NOVA does count it.

  • Every module week, you are expected to log in and submit something. Watching a video does not count on its own; submitted work does.
  • More than 3 weeks with no submitted work lowers your final grade by one letter grade, the same way unexcused absences would in a face-to-face section.
  • Week 1 matters more than you think. NOVA requires me to confirm you started the course. If you have submitted nothing by the census date (September 9), you can be administratively withdrawn — that is College policy, not mine.
  • If life is about to take a week away from you, email me ahead of time or as soon as you can. See My Goal Is an Amazing Website below for how much time that buys you.

Good news: if you work steadily every week and show real effort, I may add small communication or effort points when your final grade is right on the line between two letters.

My Goal Is an Amazing Website

My goal for you is simple. I want you to walk out of this course with a website you are proud to show people — not one that merely passed, but one you would put in front of an employer, a transfer advisor, or your family. I always want the highest and best for you, and every rule in this handbook exists to get you there, not to trip you up.

That includes the hard weeks. You are carrying a full load, and sooner or later three assignments will land on the same day. That is normal. It is not a character flaw, and it is not something you have to hide from me.

If another class collides with this one, tell me early.

Give me 24 to 48 hours of notice and I can give you more time. That is usually all it takes — one email, before the deadline, telling me what you are up against. I would rather extend a deadline than watch you turn in something rushed or nothing at all.

Less than 24 hours, and I cannot extend it. Not because I do not want to. By then the due date is on top of us and grading is already scheduled, and there is nothing left for me to move. The difference between those two outcomes is one message, sent a day earlier.

So build this habit: look at your Monday. Every Monday, open every one of your courses in Canvas and read what is due that week — all of them, not just this one. Then plan the week around the real load. Almost every extension I have had to turn down was a week nobody looked at until Thursday.

Missed Work and Deadlines

If you disappear without telling me, you are still responsible for all coursework, quizzes, and exams. It is your job to check Canvas announcements and course materials to find out what you missed.

Technical problems are not an excuse for a missed deadline. You are responsible for getting help from the right IT support.

Work Quality and Your Workspace

  • Quality counts. Spell-check and proofread your work. Run-on sentences and unedited drafts may be returned without credit.
  • Deadlines count. Follow the due dates and submission instructions posted in Canvas.
  • Submit through Canvas, in the format I asked for. Wrong file type, missing folder, or a broken link reads as an incomplete submission. Open your own submission after you upload it and check that it works.
  • Give yourself a real work session. This course needs focused blocks, not five minutes between notifications. Put the phone in another room and give the build your whole attention — the same way you would in a lab.

What I Expect From You

  • Start each module in the week it opens, not the night it closes.
  • Turn in work that shows your best effort and deliberate design choices.
  • Take part in the Canvas discussions and activities.
  • Log in several times a week so you never lose the thread.
  • If something is wrong, tell me directly so we can fix it.

If You Think a Grade Is Wrong

Seek to understand first. If you get a grade that does not look right to you, read my feedback and the rubric, then email me and tell me plainly what you expected and what you got. Bring the question, not the verdict.

I operate the same way. Before I draw a conclusion about your work, I ask you what you were trying to do. Give me that same courtesy and we will settle almost anything in one message — including the times when the mistake is mine.

Exams

  • Exams are take-home and untimed, so you can show what you actually know instead of how fast you work.
  • Exams are built around real-world tasks that match the course goals.
  • Deadlines still apply even though the exam is take-home.
  • Late exams are not accepted unless you have a documented emergency.

Turning Work In on Canvas

  • All assignments go through Canvas by the posted due date and time.
  • If you submit late, Canvas automatically takes off 20% per day.
  • Emailed assignments are not accepted unless I specifically ask for one.
  • If I gave you permission to turn something in late, email it straight to me. Please do not ask me to reopen the due date in Canvas. I know many instructors do that; for me it creates more work, not less. Just send the finished assignment to my email and I will grade it from there.
  • Submit the file I asked for, not a link to a folder I cannot open. Test your link before you submit it.
  • Check Canvas every day for updates and announcements, especially before class.

Why 11:59 PM Is a Trap

NOVA has more than 75,000 students. If you submit at the last minute, expect a late penalty. Here is what goes wrong:

  • Uploads fail because of Wi-Fi, Canvas timeouts, or browser problems.
  • Canvas slows down near deadlines because everyone is submitting at once.
  • Clock differences can mark your work late.
  • Large files like videos, ZIP folders, and images take time to upload.
  • It is easy to submit the wrong file when you are rushing.
  • There is no time left to check that your submission actually opens.
  • Stress leads to mistakes.

Do this instead: submit 30 to 60 minutes early, then open your upload to make sure it works.

Campus Closings and Zoom Sessions

Snow days do not close an online course. When the campus shuts for weather, this class keeps running and your deadlines stand — the only thing that changes is that phones and offices are dark, so email is the way to reach me. If your power or internet goes out, that is a different conversation: tell me as soon as you can get online and we will work it out. From time to time I may also hold an optional live Zoom review session. Those are announced in Canvas and are never required. I do not record them, so if you cannot make one, come to office hours or email me and I will walk you through whatever you missed.

Camera Rule for Zoom

Zoom review sessions and Zoom office hours are optional in this section, so there is no penalty for missing one. But if you do join, turn your camera on. I am talking to a person, not a black square, and it is much easier to help you when I can see what you are looking at. If your camera does not work, tell me and we will use screen share instead.

Original Work and Academic Integrity

  • Everything you turn in must be original work you created this semester. You cannot reuse work from past courses, other courses you are taking now, or earlier semesters. That is the Academic Integrity Policy.
  • You also cannot reuse the same project, media, or content across different assignments inside this course. Each assignment builds a specific skill, and reusing work skips that skill.
  • Skills and techniques carry forward. The work itself does not.

This course is designed to help you build a strong, varied portfolio. Push yourself toward new ideas, new designs, and new approaches on every assignment. Work that is not original may get a grade penalty, action under the Academic Integrity Policy, or both.

12. Thinking Machines — AI Policy

Read this one twice. The penalty here is the harshest in the course.

AI Rules for the Final Project

  1. You may only use AI after Module 9.
  2. Any AI-generated code must be commented in the code and clearly labeled as AI-assisted.
  3. Any AI-generated code must come with a clear explanation of what it does.

If you break this rule, you get a zero, and the incident is reported to Academic Affairs.

AI is a powerful tool when you use it the right way. It must not be used to skip the learning.

Learn to Use It, Not Avoid It

AI matters more and more in IT and multimedia work. Whatever you personally think about it, employers expect people entering tech careers to understand how it works, when it is appropriate, and when it is not.

In this course I use AI openly and on purpose, so you can see what responsible use looks like. When I use it, it is for building instruction: organizing lessons, making wording clearer, drafting examples, and keeping Canvas formatting consistent and accessible. That is the point: AI is a support tool, not a replacement for knowledge, skill, or thinking.

Sometimes I will ask you to use AI tools for specific multimedia tasks, like generating images, brainstorming visual ideas, or helping with production work. Those moments are planned, and I will tell you when they apply.

Never use AI to write your explanations, reflections, or any assignment meant to show what you understand. That skips the learning and defeats the purpose of the assignment.

By the end of this course you should be able to:

  • Tell the difference between appropriate and inappropriate AI use.
  • Use AI as a tool without letting it think for you.
  • Explain your work, your decisions, and your process with confidence.
  • Meet professional and ethical expectations in IT and multimedia jobs.

⚙When you need help · 9 policies

Accommodations and Accessibility Services

NOVA is committed to ensuring all students have an opportunity to pursue a college education regardless of the presence or absence of a disability. No academically qualified student with a disability will be denied access to or participation in the services, programs, and activities of the College. Your access to and inclusion in this course is important to NOVA and your professors. Please request your accommodation letter (Memorandum of Accommodations) early in the semester or as soon as you become registered so that you have adequate time to arrange your approved academic accommodations with your professors. Returning students must renew their Memorandum of Accommodations (MOA) every semester; these students should submit the request 24 hours or later after enrolling in at least one class. Allow up to 7 business days for the request to be approved.

Accommodations are provided for in-person, online, and remote/synchronous (Zoom) learning. To get started, review NOVA’s Accommodation and Accessibility Services website. Following a meeting with a counselor, you will be issued a Memorandum of Accommodation (MOA). You must provide your MOA to your professors, testing proctor, and/or tutoring center to receive your accommodation. You may provide your MOA any time during the semester; however, accommodations are not retroactive. You may email your MOA to your professors or provide them with a printed copy. They will send you an email to acknowledge receipt. You and your professors should schedule a meeting outside of class to discuss questions regarding your MOA. Please remind your professors of any special arrangements that must be made in advance of tests and assessments. If you need a sign language interpreter, or if you need live captions for your Zoom class, send an email to interpreters@nvcc.edu.

Your ability to fully participate in this course matters. If you experience any difficulty accessing course content, activities, or technology, please contact me as soon as possible so that we can address the issue together. Accessibility is a shared responsibility, and your feedback helps ensure that all students have access to learning.

Tutoring

NOVA’s Tutoring Centers offer free in-person and virtual tutoring to all NOVA Nighthawks. Students can drop by any one of campus Tutoring Centers for walk-in services or set up an appointment for tutoring. To request an appointment for one-on-one tutoring, either in-person or via Zoom, log in to myNOVA to select EAB Navigate. For more information and for Tutoring Center locations, visit Tutoring & Academic Support. In addition, 24/7 online tutoring (via Brainfuse) is free to all students. To access online tutoring, click on the 24/7 Tutoring link located in your Canvas course in the course navigation menu.

Libraries

NOVA Libraries support the mission of the College to deliver in-person and online postsecondary teaching, learning, and workforce development to students, faculty, staff and community members. The libraries promote equity and inclusion by addressing systemic barriers to student success and fostering intellectual curiosity, creativity and critical thinking. At our libraries, you may borrow books/printed material, access article databases, access videos, connect to Wi-Fi, use the printers, and reserve a study room.

Office of Wellness and Mental Health

During your time at NOVA, you may experience challenges including struggles with academics or your personal well-being. NOVA has support resources available. Please contact the Office of Wellness and Mental Health if you are seeking resources and support, or if you are worried about a friend or classmate.

Financial Stability and Advocacy Centers

The Financial Stability and Advocacy Center provides assistance to students who are experiencing financial hardships that might prevent the students’ academic success. The personnel at the Financial Stability and Advocacy Centers work with students to identify college or community services available. For more information, please visit the Financial Stability and Advocacy Center webpage, or contact the office by calling 703.323.3450 or emailing financialstability@nvcc.edu.

Remote Student Support Services

If you need academic assistance or need college services but cannot make it to campus, many of our services can be accessed remotely. We can provide assistance from several departments, including the following:

  • Academic Advising
  • Canvas and Course Resources (guides and tutorials)
  • Financial Aid
  • IT Help Desk
  • Library Support
Career Services

The NOVA Career Services Office helps students explore career paths, build professional skills, and connect with employers. Whether you’re choosing a major, preparing your resume or cover letter, searching for internships, or getting ready for your first job after graduation, our career counselors and coaches provide guidance and resources to help you succeed. Join Handshake to discover and apply for jobs and internships; connect with employers; access professional development resources; and request career counseling services.

Forms to Request Services and Assistance

NOVA’s Forms Library is where you can access forms frequently used by the College. The forms are available in Portable Document Format (.pdf), Online or Excel. Some of the forms you will find online include:

  • Accommodations and Accessibility Services: Request for Alternate Format
  • Course grade appeal
  • Enrollment Services: Course Repeat Request
  • Enrollment Services: Enrollment with Permission
  • Financial Aid: Satisfactory Academic Progress (SAP) Appeal Form
  • Parking Services: Vehicle Registration Form
  • Student Grievance Forms
  • Veteran Enrollment Request Form (VERF)

You also have the option to Make a Report to the college. Here is the list of reports you can submit:

  • Report a student needed assistance (non-conduct).
  • Report an academic integrity violation.
  • Report a student conduct violation (non-academic integrity).
  • Report a threat assessment.
  • Report Sexual Misconduct (Title IX).
  • Title IX Pregnant and Parenting Accommodation Request.
  • Ombuds Assistance Request — student may email OMBUDS@nvcc.edu.
Student Ombuds Services (SOS)

For students who believe an unfair resolution was made for a formal complaint made to NVCC (i.e., academic concerns, ethical behavior, violation of College policies and/or procedures, business services, financial aid, etc.), SOS will investigate the student’s concern.

  • Confidential — students may discuss problems or issues in a confidential manner
  • Independent — of any individual/office within NVCC
  • Informal — review matters received and make informal inquiries to offer resolution options, make referrals, and mediate disputes.
  • Neutral — strives for impartiality, fairness, and objectivity in the treatment of people and the consideration of issues
  • Voluntary — it is the student’s responsibility to contact SOS for services

Contact: Dr. Tanneh Kamara, Coordinator, Student Ombuds Services (SOS), Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities. Phone: 703-530-2834. Email: ombuds@nvcc.edu.

⏳Money, dates, and staying enrolled · 5 policies

Important Dates

The academic calendar provides information about important dates and deadlines each semester. Visit this calendar to learn about:

  • Open registration dates.
  • Academic advising dates.
  • Registration dates.
  • Deadlines to pay tuition fees.
  • First and Last day of classes
  • Deadline to drop the class with a tuition refund or change classes to audit.
  • Deadline to withdraw without grade penalty (W) and no refund.
  • Final Exams Schedule.
  • Breaks and holidays.
  • Financial aid disbursement dates.
  • Deadline to apply for graduation.
Course Drop/Withdrawal Policy

Please note these important deadlines related to your enrollment in a course:

  • Students may drop courses through myNOVA until the last day to drop with a tuition refund (census date). Students who drop a class during this period will receive a full refund.
  • Requests to change your grade status to audit must also be completed before the last day to drop with a tuition refund (census date).
  • Students who do not attend at least one class meeting or participate in an online learning class by the last day to drop with a tuition refund (census date) may be administratively withdrawn from the class. This means that there will be no record of the class or any letter grade on the student’s transcript. The student’s tuition will not be refunded.
  • The Last Day to Withdraw is the last day to withdraw from classes without a grade penalty. Students will receive a grade of W. Students may withdraw from a course through myNOVA. The student’s tuition will not be refunded. Withdrawing from a course after the census date and before the withdrawal date will result in a “W” grade appearing on your transcript.

To identify these important dates for your courses, please visit the College Academic Calendar and scroll down to the specific session for your course. Please note that any drops or withdrawals from a course may impact financial aid, international student status, or military benefits. Students with questions should check with the appropriate offices.

Enrollment Cancellation
  • Students who do not make payment arrangements for their courses will be dropped.
  • Students dropped for nonpayment cannot be enrolled in a course after the Last Day to Add/Drop, even if they have attended the class and completed coursework. Only students who were dropped due to college error are eligible for late enrollment (enrollment after the Last Day to Add/Drop).
  • See NOVA Payment Options.
NOVA All Access

NOVA All Access is the default way to obtain your required course materials (physical and/or digital) at NOVA.

  • You are automatically enrolled when you register for classes.
  • A fee of $22.50 per credit hour is added to your student account. This fee appears along with your tuition and other charges.
  • All Access only applies to students in college credit courses. Students in contracted dual enrollment courses and students in NOVA’s non-credit workforce and professional development courses are not participating in All Access.

Compare the cost of All Access with buying materials on your own. If All Access costs more than other options, then opt out of the program. All Access is optional, but remember:

  • You can opt out each semester, but your decision applies to all your classes that semester.
  • You can opt out (or opt back in) only at certain times.
  • If you opt out, the fee will be refunded. If you opt back in, the fee is added again.

If your course uses OER materials (for “open educational resources”) or is “no materials required,” your instructor will let you know the best way to obtain your course materials. You may not be required to purchase textbooks and other materials for this course. We are making this information available so you can make an informed choice about participating in NOVA’s course materials program, NOVA All Access.

The opt-out window for All Access for Fall 2026 opens on July 27, 2026 and closes on your earliest census date.

Through the All-Access program, most physical books are rentals. Plan to return your rental books to the campus bookstore at the end of each semester. If you have rental books that you have not returned from a previous semester, please return those as well. To find the specific dates for your session, view NOVA’s Academic Calendar.

Prerequisite Verification Statement

As noted in the Course Prerequisites Policy, some courses have prerequisite or corequisite requirements that are established to foster a student’s success in the course. Students may not enroll in a course for which they do not meet the prerequisites by the time the course begins or for which they do not simultaneously enroll in any corequisite. Students may be administratively dropped from any course for which they have not met the prerequisite. If a course has a prerequisite, it is the responsibility of the student to ensure completion of this pre-requisite course first. Any student needing assistance in determining prerequisite or corequisite requirements can reach out to their faculty member or Campus Academic Division office for support.

⚖How we treat each other · 4 policies

Academic Integrity Policy

NOVA promotes and emphasizes the importance of honesty in academic work. It is therefore imperative for students to maintain the highest standard of honor in their scholastic work.

Academic dishonesty, as outlined in more detail in the Academic Integrity Policy (Policy Number: 224), can include, but is not limited to cheating on an exam or quiz, submitting work that is not your own (plagiarism), or sharing assessments online. Additionally, the use of AI to complete assigned work may be considered a violation of the academic integrity policy. Students are urged to be cautious when using any web tools designed to assist with assignments without their instructors’ explicit permission to do so and to cite their sources in all their work.

Consequences of academic dishonesty can include a failing grade on an assignment, a failing grade in the course, and may include additional administrative sanctions such as suspension or expulsion from the college. Procedures for disciplinary measures and appeals are outlined in the Academic Integrity Procedures. It is a student’s responsibility to become familiar with the student code of conduct. Lack of awareness is no excuse for noncompliance with NOVA’s policies and procedures.

NOVA faculty may choose to use tools such as Turnitin to detect and flag instances of plagiarism in academic writing.

Student Integrity and Conduct

Investigate alleged violations of the Student Code of Conduct.

  • Adjudication of informal and formal Code of Conduct hearings
  • Mediation (settling differences)
  • Student development workshops
  • Professional development workshop on topics like Conflict Resolution and Classroom Management
  • Referrals to resources and services
Student Rights and Responsibilities

The Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities (OSRR) promotes and encourages honesty, integrity, and respect among NOVA students and staff. We accomplish our mission through education, compliance through behavioral standards, and support of individual rights. Our work helps enhance the quality of the NOVA community and equips students with the knowledge, skills, and resources to be successful inside and outside of the classroom.

Title IX

Title IX is a civil rights law that prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in educational programs, activities, admission, and employment. Complaints of sex-based discrimination, sexual violence, domestic violence, dating violence, and sexual or gender-based harassment are governed by the Title IX Policy. For more information or to make a report, visit the Office of Title IX.

✉Staying in the loop · 2 policies

Communication

Northern Virginia Community College (NVCC) faculty, staff, and administrators communicate with students through their official NVCC email accounts. Students are likewise required to use their VCCS email accounts to communicate with instructors and other college personnel. Students should check their email accounts regularly. Keep your contact information current in SIS.

Closing Information

NOVA announces campus and college closings on the NOVA homepage. You can also receive notification by cell phone or email if you register for NOVA Alert. Also review NOVA’s guidance on emergency closings, delayed openings, and continuation of instruction.

If a course is canceled due to a weather event or other unforeseen situation, check the course Canvas site or NOVA email as soon as possible for instructions and assignments to avoid falling behind in coursework.

One last thing

Why All of This Exists

I want the highest and best for my students.

Every policy in this handbook — the deadlines, the weekly check-ins, the 24 to 48 hours, the way we talk to each other — is here for one reason: to make sure you succeed. None of it was written to catch you out or to make my life easier. It was written because I have watched what helps students finish this course with something they are proud of, and this is that list.

Structure is not the opposite of care. It is the care. The deadlines keep you from falling so far behind that the climb back stops feeling possible. Showing up on time keeps you in the room where the building actually happens. Talking to me early is what lets me say yes.

So read the rules, keep them, and then forget about them and go build something good. I am on your side for the whole fifteen weeks. Come find me when you need me.

Let’s build something amazing. — Dr. G
